title: Probability & Statistics
weightage: 11–18 marks (≈18 in 2025 with 12 Qs, 11 in 2026 with 7 Qs); highest-weight maths subject in DA
summary: The single biggest maths block in GATE DA: expect NAT-heavy questions on conditional probability/Bayes, expectation & variance, named distributions (normal, exponential, uniform, Poisson, binomial), conditional expectation from joint PDFs, plus a few inferential-stats questions (CLT, confidence intervals, z/t/chi-squared tests). Speed with standard results (memoryless property, E/Var tables, standard-normal symmetry) decides marks.
notesGuide: 1) Download the MIT 18.05 (Spring 2022) class reading PDFs from the 'Classes, Reading and In-Class Materials' page: Class 1b, 2, 3, 4a, 4b, 5a–5d, 6a, 6b, 7a, 7b, 17b, 18, 19, 22 cover essentially the whole GATE DA syllabus — print these, they are short (5–15 pages each) and exam-aligned. 2) Keep the free Blitzstein & Hwang 'Introduction to Probability' PDF (probabilitybook.net) as the reference book for harder problems (Ch 1–7, 9, 10). 3) For inferential statistics (CI, z/t/chi-squared tests, sampling distributions) use OpenIntro Statistics (free PDF) Ch 5–7 or NPTEL Somesh Kumar weeks 8–12. 4) Make your own short notes as a 2–3 page formula sheet: one table of every distribution (PMF/PDF, CDF, mean, variance, MGF-free key property such as memorylessness), one page of identities (total probability, Bayes, law of total expectation/variance, Var(aX+bY), Cov/Corr properties), and one page of test-selection rules (z vs t vs chi-squared, df, one/two-tailed, CI formulas). 5) While solving PYQs on GATE Overflow, log every trap you fall into (e.g. confusing independence with mutual exclusion, mean vs rate parametrisation of exponential) in an 'error log' at the end of the notes and revise it weekly.

subtopics: Type I and Type II errors
One- and two-tailed z-test for mean/proportion

topics.tips: Pick the test from what is known: σ known/large n → z; σ unknown small n → t (df n−1); categorical counts → chi-squared (df = k−1 or (r−1)(c−1)). Questions are typically conceptual or one-step numerical.
